video_title: ⏭️ Forward Deployed: Voice AI on what works in 2026
gist: Latent Space launches a Forward Deployed spinoff hosted by Basil, replaying a panel with engineers from Vapi, Smallest AI, Daily/Pipecat, Decagon and Retell on how production voice agents are actually built in 2026: cascaded speech-to-text/LLM/text-to-speech pipelines still beat native voice-to-voice models on reliability and guardrails, latency/cost/intelligence tradeoffs dominate architecture choices, and prompt-engineering best practice has swung back toward giving models full context as frontier LLM reliability improves.

insights.claim: As of this recording, the state-of-the-art production architecture for voice agents is still a three-step cascaded pipeline (speech-to-text, then LLM, then text-to-speech) rather than a native voice-to-voice model, because voice-to-voice models are not yet reliable enough for production use.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: Investors should discount pure-play voice-to-voice model startups on near-term enterprise reliability and favor vendors that architect cascaded pipelines with guardrails as the deployable product today.
insights.quote: the reality is those just are not super reliable right now

insights.claim: A basic cascaded voice agent pipeline routes voice input through a transport layer (WebRTC, phone, or websockets), then speech-to-text with background-noise removal and voice isolation, then a voice-activity-detection plus 'smart turn' model to detect when the speaker has finished, then an LLM (which may issue tool calls), then text-to-speech streamed back over the same transport.
insights.speaker: Brun (Daily/Pipecat)
insights.so_what: This is the baseline reference architecture investors should use to evaluate any voice-agent infrastructure vendor's technical claims and differentiation.

insights.claim: Speech-to-speech models were originally pursued because converting speech to text loses emotional/tonal information, and because the human brain processes conversation asynchronously (forming responses while still listening) rather than in the synchronous listen-then-respond loop of a cascaded pipeline; the tradeoff is that speech-to-speech encoders currently have worse transcription accuracy than dedicated speech-to-text models.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: Accuracy-vs-naturalness is the key axis to underwrite when comparing speech-to-speech model vendors; interpretability research (making the model less of a black box) is the near-term lever for closing the accuracy gap.

insights.claim: Smallest AI built 'Hydra,' a multimodal speech-to-speech model that takes in and outputs both speech and text simultaneously (unlike Sesame's pure speech-in/speech-out design), specifically so that tool-calling and guardrails are not lost when moving away from a cascaded architecture.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: Product differentiation in the speech-to-speech category is emerging around retaining enterprise controllability (tool calls, guardrails), not just conversational naturalness — a filter for evaluating competing S2S models.

insights.claim: The likely medium-term outcome is a hybrid architecture: a speech-to-speech model handles the live conversational loop and autopilot-type answers, but delegates to a cascaded multi-LLM pipeline (via an interrupt/semaphore-like mechanism) whenever the query is complex enough to require a lookup or specialized reasoning.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: Vendors that can seamlessly interleave speech-to-speech and cascaded execution paths, rather than picking one architecture exclusively, are best positioned as the category matures.

insights.claim: Sesame's viral speech-to-speech demo did not convert into a sustained enterprise voice product; the panel's understanding is that the company pivoted to building hardware (possibly glasses) with former voice/hardware hires, reportedly because its CEO had already made significant money and wanted to pursue a passion project rather than compete commercially.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: A flashy voice-to-voice demo does not automatically translate into an enterprise business model; investors should distinguish demo virality from a defensible commercial voice-AI product.
insights.quote: the CEO had already made a ton of money and he just really wants to play around basically

insights.claim: Voice agent builders must explicitly trade off response intelligence against latency: smarter/larger model responses take longer, which can be good or bad depending on the use case, so architecture choice is use-case-specific rather than a single 'best' model.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: There is no universal 'best' model for voice; evaluate vendors on how they tune the intelligence/latency dial per use case rather than on raw model benchmarks alone.

insights.claim: Production voice agent teams maintain a 'waterfall' of fallback LLM providers so that if one frontier LLM's infrastructure goes down (e.g., Anthropic's Opus), the voice agent keeps functioning rather than failing completely.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor LLM redundancy is now table stakes for production voice infrastructure, implying real demand for orchestration/failover layers independent of any single model vendor's uptime.
insights.quote: what do you do when opus goes down?

insights.claim: Turn-taking (knowing when a caller has actually finished speaking versus just pausing to think) is a nontrivial, still-unsolved problem in voice AI that requires dedicated voice-activity-detection plus a 'smart turn' model, not simple silence detection.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: Turn-taking/interruption handling remains a differentiable technical moat rather than a solved commodity feature — worth diligencing specifically when evaluating voice infra vendors.

insights.claim: For fast, non-thinking cascaded pipeline steps, Gemini 2.5 is preferred over the newer Gemini 3.5 because it is noticeably faster, and Claude's Haiku model is also considered very good quality but still slower than desired for real-time voice.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: A concrete, name-specific mid-2026 signal that newer/larger model releases are not automatically preferred in latency-sensitive production voice pipelines — speed-per-dollar can beat raw capability upgrades for this workload.
insights.quote: I still like my Gemini 2.5 really well. Like it's so fast.

insights.claim: Deliberately inserted contextual filler words (e.g., 'just give me a sec') are used to mask latency during slow steps like a 5-second customer API tool call; testing showed that having zero fillers can actually feel more rigid to users than well-executed natural fillers.
insights.speaker: guest (voice AI panel)
insights.so_what: Filler-word design is a measurable, testable UX lever for masking latency in voice products — a low-cost, high-leverage feature to check for in vendor demos.

insights.claim: Because most abandoned calls hang up within about 10 seconds, and large system prompts still get billed in full as input tokens on every call, splitting large prompts into smaller specialized sub-agent prompts (e.g., a dedicated agent just for capturing payment info) reduces both latency and token cost simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Stephen (Vapi)
insights.so_what: Cost efficiency in voice AI is being driven by prompt decomposition, not just model choice — a concrete unit-economics lever investors should look for in vendor architecture.

insights.claim: Smallest AI trains and offers a proprietary small fine-tuned language model called 'Electron' for real-time voice use cases, which customers increasingly pair with better knowledge-base/memory systems in place of general-purpose realtime models like GPT-4o/4.1, citing lower cost, lower latency, higher reliability, and freedom from third-party API latency spikes that come with no direct control over scaling.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: Self-hosted/fine-tuned small models are displacing general-purpose realtime APIs in cost- and latency-sensitive voice deployments — a specific competitive threat to OpenAI's realtime voice API business and a positive signal for vertical small-model vendors.

themes.theme: Prompt and context engineering for voice

insights.claim: Voice AI teams solved conversation-context 'compaction' (trimming/summarizing state before hitting the context limit) years before coding-agent builders encountered the same problem, because early voice models had very small context windows (10,000-50,000 tokens) and would 'go off the rails' after roughly five to ten conversational turns.
insights.speaker: Brun (Daily/Pipecat)
insights.so_what: Voice AI engineering practice is a leading indicator for general agent context-management techniques; teams building coding/agentic products can mine voice-AI playbooks for compaction strategies already battle-tested at scale.

insights.claim: LLMs disproportionately attend to the first and last roughly 4% of a prompt and tend to forget content in the middle, so placing critical information (e.g., a return policy) mid-prompt makes hallucination likely.
insights.speaker: Brun (Daily/Pipecat)
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable prompt-engineering rule: critical policy/rule content should be placed at the start or end of a system prompt, not buried in the middle.
insights.quote: LLMs are you know goofy in that sense that always remember the first 4% and the last 4% and everything in between they kind of forget

insights.claim: Optimal prompt structure is use-case dependent: predictable inbound flows (where the conversation path can be anticipated) favor a node/graph-based workflow approach, while unpredictable outbound flows (where callers respond erratically) favor a single large unified 'central brain' prompt that can flexibly draw on any component as needed.
insights.speaker: Stephen (Vapi)
insights.so_what: There is no single correct prompt architecture for voice agents; investors evaluating agent-building platforms should check whether the vendor supports both graph-based and monolithic-prompt approaches rather than forcing one paradigm.

insights.claim: Practice has swung back toward giving the LLM the entire prompt and letting it figure out relevance, rather than pre-filtering which rules/prompt snippets are 'situationally relevant,' because frontier LLM reliability has improved enough over roughly the last seven months that dynamic situational filtering is now often less reliable than just including everything.
insights.speaker: guest (voice AI panel)
insights.so_what: This is a real reversal in engineering best practice within roughly half a year, signaling that context-window and instruction-following gains in frontier models are outpacing the value of manual context-optimization tooling — a headwind for startups selling dynamic prompt-optimization middleware.
insights.quote: sometimes the reliability of deciding when these things are relevant or not is actually worse than just giving all of it to the model

themes.theme: Voice AI market structure and competition

insights.claim: Customer support call centers represent hundreds of billions of dollars of spend industry-wide and are broadly considered low quality today, which is framed as the core market opportunity underlying voice-agent vendors like Decagon.
insights.speaker: host (Latent Space)
insights.so_what: Total addressable market framing for voice-AI customer support vendors: the comparison point is a massive, chronically underperforming incumbent spend base, not a small niche.
insights.quote: hundreds of billions of dollars spent on this stuff and they're all you know bad

insights.claim: Sierra has publicly described voice agents as one of the most competitive markets in AI right now.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: Independent competitive-landscape confirmation (from a well-funded rival, Sierra) that voice agents are a crowded, high-intensity category — useful for competitive-mapping and valuation benchmarking.

insights.claim: The strongest signal that cascaded pipelines remain necessary comes not from vendors selling voice pipelines (who have an obvious incentive to claim their approach is state-of-the-art) but from forward-deployed engineers actually running customer-facing deployments, who independently conclude that speech-to-speech models 'are not there yet' and 'may never be,' while researchers keep pushing for bigger models to solve everything.
insights.speaker: host (Latent Space)
insights.so_what: Weight the technology assessments of customer-facing engineers (least incentive to oversell) more heavily than vendor marketing or pure research claims when judging voice-AI technology readiness.
insights.quote: the models are not there yet. They may never be.

insights.claim: In outbound calling use cases, a large share of call recipients hang up almost immediately once they realize they are talking to a bot, regardless of model quality.
insights.speaker: Basil
insights.so_what: Outbound voice AI faces a persistent behavioral adoption barrier that better models alone will not fix; disclosure/framing strategy and use-case selection (e.g., debt collection where the call is expected) matter as much as model quality.
insights.quote: whenever somebody like picks up the phone and you do an outbound use case, a lot of the times they just hang up as soon as they realize it's a bot

insights.claim: Inbound and outbound voice bots require fundamentally different guardrail designs: outbound bots (e.g., debt collection) can simply drop the call if the human goes off-script since the bot fully controls the conversation's purpose and has no obligation to continue, whereas inbound bots have little control over caller intent and must handle far more open-ended, unpredictable requests (e.g., an Amazon-scale bot needing different policies per product category).
insights.speaker: Brun (Daily/Pipecat)
insights.so_what: Risk and complexity profiles differ sharply by call direction; underwrite outbound deployments as lower engineering risk/higher adoption friction, and inbound deployments as higher engineering complexity but better user acceptance.

insights.claim: Smallest AI's speech-to-speech model is deliberately kept English-only for now because the underlying technology is still frontier and not yet mainstream; on the cascaded side, the company sees heavy multilingual demand from India and Latin America, while US demand is mostly English with some Spanish, and noise cancellation (not accent handling) is described as the remaining 'last mile' problem for English deployments.
insights.speaker: Sudarian (Smallest AI)
insights.so_what: Emerging-market demand (India, LatAm) is a real, named growth vector for cascaded voice-AI deployment today, ahead of speech-to-speech multilingual maturity.

insights.claim: Text-to-speech providers considered state-of-the-art for English, Spanish, and Portuguese completely failed to work for a Japan deployment, and Arabic pronunciation of brand names and addresses is particularly difficult, which is why Vapi lets customers bring their own custom TTS server rather than relying on one universal voice stack.
insights.speaker: Stephen (Vapi)
insights.so_what: Voice quality is highly language/locale-specific, so platform architecture that supports bring-your-own-TTS is a real differentiator for global enterprise deployments versus single-vendor voice stacks.
insights.quote: what we thought it was state-of-the-art for um something like English, Spanish, Portuguese ... didn't work at all

insights.claim: Vapi publishes open-source, turn-based benchmarks separately for speech-to-text, LLM, and text-to-speech components (with the underlying test turns fully open), so that when a new model launches — such as Nvidia's Nemotron ASR model, benchmarked the same day it launched — builders can immediately test it against standardized turns, run it locally, or compare it to self-hosted infrastructure rather than relying on vendor claims.
insights.speaker: Stephen (Vapi)
insights.so_what: Open, component-level benchmarking is becoming a competitive and trust-building tool in voice AI; investors should watch which infra vendors publish reproducible benchmarks versus those that only make marketing claims.
